Learning to Optimize
through Solver-Grounded
Self-Play

Xia Jiang1  Yaoxin Wu1  Chenyu Zhou2

Mengzhu Xu1  Wim P.M. Nuijten1  Yingqian Zhang1

1Eindhoven University of Technology

2Shanghai Jiaotong University

 

1  Introduction

Optimization modeling stands at the core of decision-making across diverse industrial sectors, ranging from supply chain planning (Nurjanni et al., 2017; Kochakkashani et al., 2023), healthcare scheduling (Earnshaw and Dennett, 2003; Nabavizadeh et al., 2024), to portfolio optimization (Hegade et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2024). Traditionally, this process requires translating complex problems into mathematical formulations and then implementing them in solver-specific languages, which demands significant human effort and expertise (Li et al., 2025a; Le et al., 2026). Recently, the advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has begun to reshape this landscape. Leveraging their language understanding and code generation capabilities, LLMs have enhanced the automation of the modeling process (Xiao et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025a; Yazdani et al., 2025). This shift not only streamlines the translation from problem descriptions to formulations, but also makes optimization modeling and solving accessible to a broader range of non-experts (Kadıoğlu et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025b).

LLM-based optimization modeling has technically shifted from inference-time prompt engineering toward training specialized models on optimization-specific data. Initial efforts successfully designed sophisticated workflows and prompt templates to guide LLMs through the modeling process (Xiao et al., 2024; AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024; Astorga et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). This line of work elicits the latent reasoning potential of general-purpose LLMs by operating within frozen parameters, which may limit the model’s ability to deeply internalize specialized optimization knowledge. Consequently, a growing body of recent work focuses on fine-tuning base models with human-crafted, domain-specific datasets to achieve better modeling capabilities (Jiang et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Lima et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2026; Min et al., 2026).

The efficacy of fine-tuning paradigms fundamentally depends on the availability of high-quality datasets (Bukharin et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). This dependence is particularly problematic for optimization modeling, where collecting training data requires not only diverse problem descriptions, but also corresponding mathematically valid formulations and solver-verified solutions. The scarcity of high-quality supervised training examples and the prohibitive overhead of expert annotation constrain the scalability of Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) (Xiao et al., 2025). As illustrated in Table 1, existing research, ranging from offline SFT frameworks (Yang et al., 2025b) to online Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches (Chen et al., 2025a), has advanced by leveraging curated training instances that pair natural-language problem descriptions with solver-callable formulations. These instances are typically synthesized with expert intervention (Yang et al., 2025b; Jiang et al., 2025a) or distilled from teacher models such as GPT-4 (Huang et al., 2025). While establishing strong baselines, their heavy reliance on external training datasets introduces two critical limitations. The first is Generalization Ceiling: models trained on human-curated datasets are prone to overfitting specific modeling conventions or solver-dependent syntactic patterns, which undermines their robustness in unseen settings (e.g., when adopting a solver unseen during training) (Li et al., 2025a). The second, more fundamental limitation is Capability Anchoring: static supervision intrinsically ties the model’s reasoning capability to the proficiency of annotators, either human experts or contemporary teacher LLMs. As LLMs advance rapidly, existing datasets may lose training value and risk becoming “obsolete” as the reasoning capabilities of LLMs surpass the complexities represented in them. Beyond static dataset curation, LLMs should autonomously explore the optimization landscape, generate problems, and leverage solver feedback as learning guidance. In this regard, a self-evolving training loop is envisioned that continuously expands the model’s competence in optimization modeling.

To remove this dependence on externally curated supervision while retaining reliable solver-grounded feedback, we propose OPT-Zero, a self-play training framework that eliminates the need for human-annotated or teacher-generated data entirely. OPT-Zero operates through a dual-role RL-based training process where a single LLM alternately assumes the roles of Proposer and Solver, engaged in a continuous closed-loop learning. In each iteration, the Proposer generates new optimization problem instances designed to challenge the current capabilities of the Solver. The Solver attempts to formulate models and execute code to solve these instances, receiving feedback from external optimization solvers (e.g., Gurobi, CPLEX). This solver-grounded feedback serves as the reward signal for RL, enabling the LLM to adapt to increasing problem complexity and alternately update the Proposer and Solver policies. As training progresses, the Proposer learns to synthesize more valid and challenging problems, while the Solver progressively enhances its modeling proficiency to overcome the harder problems. As demonstrated in our experiments, the self-play training creates an auto-curriculum that mitigates issues of generalization ceilings and capability anchoring in static datasets, resulting in competitive performance without relying on annotated data (see Figure 1).

Our contributions are summarized as follows.

1) To the authors’ knowledge, this is the first study on fine-tuning LLMs for optimization modeling through a fully self-play paradigm. OPT-Zero requires no external training data, eliminating costly expert annotation or teacher LLM distillation, on which previous approaches heavily depend.

2) We develop a solver-grounded RL framework that jointly trains problem generation and solving in a closed loop. OPT-Zero alternates between proposing and solving problems, while external solver execution provides reward signals that guide policy updates, forming a mutually reinforcing pipeline.

3) Without any curated training data, OPT-Zero can match or even surpass the performance of state-of-the-art data-dependent methods, while showing strong generalizability under different settings, establishing self-play as a scalable training paradigm for advancing LLM in optimization.

2  Related Work

LLMs for Optimization Modeling. The task of automatically translating natural-language problem descriptions into mathematical programs was formally introduced in the NeurIPS2022 Competition (Ramamonjison et al., 2023). Since then, there has been a growing interest in leveraging LLMs for optimization and solver-oriented code generation. Existing approaches can be broadly divided into two paradigms: prompt-based and training-based methods. Early prompt-based efforts focused on improving LLM performance through prompt engineering (Wasserkrug et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a). Subsequent work moved beyond simple prompting to construct more structured pipelines, incorporating strategies such as multi-agent collaboration (Xiao et al., 2024; AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), Monte-Carlo tree search (Astorga et al., 2025), and retrieval-augmented generation (Jiang et al., 2025c; Liu et al., 2025). Despite improved inference-time reasoning, these methods operate on frozen LLM parameters and thus heavily rely on strong base models. In contrast, training-based methods aim to internalize domain knowledge by fine-tuning on domain-specific datasets (Huang et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025a; Ma et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). This paradigm enables small models to acquire specialized modeling skills. However, its effectiveness fundamentally depends on the availability of high-quality data. To alleviate the data bottleneck, recent studies have devoted effort to dataset synthesis pipelines (Li et al., 2025b; Lu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b). Unlike existing paradigms, we eliminate curated supervision from human-annotated or teacher-generated data entirely through self-play, in which LLM modeling capabilities emerge through solver-grounded interactions.

Self-Play Training in LLMs. Self-play training generalizes the AlphaZero paradigm (Silver et al., 2018) to open-ended domains, improving LLMs through interaction with copies of themselves or their own outputs. Chen et al. (2024b) formalized self-play fine-tuning, showing that a model can bootstrap quality improvements by distinguishing its own previous generations from human-written references, without any new human annotations. Beyond alleviating data scarcity, self-play is also motivated by the availability of cheap automatic verifiers in executable domains (e.g., coding) (Haluptzok et al., 2023; Wilf et al., 2025) and by the goal of surpassing static supervised datasets via self-generated curricula (Lin et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026). In reasoning-intensive domains such as mathematics and code generation, self-play has been combined with RL to yield strong results (Wu et al., 2025; Jayalath et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025). Our self-play framework differs from prior work as follows: 1) we focus on optimization modeling and decompose learning into two roles: a Proposer that generates optimization problems and a Solver that formulates and solves them. As a result, the trained model serves dual roles, as both a problem generator and a solver; 2) instead of relying on a fixed task distribution, the Proposer continuously synthesizes new problems. Their difficulty is regulated by a reference buffer with difficulty-aware sampling, producing a self-generated curriculum that co-evolves with the Solver’s capability; 3) both roles are grounded in solver-based verification, which provides RL reward signals and enables the LLM to adapt to increasing problem complexity.

3  Methodology

We parameterize a single LLM with weights θ\theta that is shared between two roles: a Proposer with policy πθP\pi_{\theta}^{P} and a Solver with policy πθS\pi_{\theta}^{S}. Given a context prompt, πθP\pi_{\theta}^{P} generates a new optimization problem, comprising a natural-language description, a formal mathematical model (e.g., a linear programming formulation), and executable solver-calling code. After that, πθS\pi_{\theta}^{S} receives only the natural-language description of the problem and independently reconstructs the formulation and corresponding code solution. Under the OPT-Zero framework, the two roles form a mutually reinforcing learning loop. As the Proposer improves, it generates more diverse and challenging problems that expose the Solver to richer scenarios. As the Solver becomes stronger, easy problems provide diminishing training value, which in turn drives the Proposer to produce harder instances. Crucially, the Proposer is trained to generate valid formulations and code, thus directly enhancing the Solver’s modeling ability. Conversely, by reconstructing formulations from natural language, the Solver training strengthens the model’s structural reasoning, implicitly enabling the Proposer to produce more valid and well-formed problems. This mutual knowledge transfer between two roles, enabled by shared weights θ\theta, is a key advantage of our self-play training framework, eliminating the need for annotators or teacher models.

The training process alternates between optimizing πθP\pi_{\theta}^{P} and πθS\pi_{\theta}^{S} via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) over TT iterations. Figure 2 illustrates the framework with the full loop detailed in Section 3.4.

3.1  Problem Formulation

Optimization Problem Representation. We consider Linear, Integer, and Mixed-integer Linear Programs (LP/IP/MILP) as the target problem classes in line with the mainstream literature (Xiao et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025a; Zhou et al., 2026). Formally, a problem instance is represented as a tuple 𝒫=(σ,f,𝒱,𝒞,s)\mathcal{P}=(\sigma,f,\mathcal{V},\mathcal{C},s), where σ∈{min,max}\sigma\in\{\min,\max\} is the optimization sense, ff is the objective expression over a set of decision variables 𝒱\mathcal{V}, 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a set of constraints, and ss is a natural-language description that presents 𝒫\mathcal{P} as a practical decision-making scenario without exposing the solution. We use 𝒫∗=f∗\mathcal{P}^{*}=f^{*} to denote the optimal objective for 𝒫\mathcal{P}, which is often obtained by a solver (e.g., Gurobi).

Proposer Output. Given a prompt with in-context reference problems sampled from the reference buffer ℬ\mathcal{B}, the Proposer (πθP\pi_{\theta}^{P}) is trained to generate a structured completion consisting of the problem tuple 𝒫\mathcal{P} and the corresponding executable solver-calling code that can produce 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*}. Therefore, the Proposer is required to not only generate problems but also provide their solutions in executable code.

Solver Output. The solver (πθS\pi_{\theta}^{S}) receives only the natural-language description ss of a problem 𝒫\mathcal{P} and must independently produce a two-part output: a reconstructed mathematical model, which is defined by (σ,f,𝒱,𝒞)(\sigma,f,\mathcal{V},\mathcal{C}), and an executable solver-calling code block. Crucially, πθS\pi_{\theta}^{S} has no access to Proposer’s formulation (i.e., mathematical model) during generation. The code-level correctness is assessed by comparing the objective value returned by the executed code against 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*}, while the declared mathematical model is verified separately for the model-level reward (as detailed below).

Solver-Grounded Verification. A central challenge in self-play is obtaining a verified solution, against which the LLM (both Proposer and Solver) outputs can be evaluated. Since the two roles generate mathematical model and code during training, we establish verification processes for optimization modeling and coding, respectively: 1) For optimization modeling, we employ a canonical verifier that independently constructs and solves the mathematical model from the generated model fields (σ,f,𝒱,𝒞)(\sigma,f,\mathcal{V},\mathcal{C}) using a canonical solver (e.g., Gurobi). The resulting optimal value 𝒫∗=f∗\mathcal{P}^{*}=f^{*}, if exists, serves as the ground-truth objective for the given problem specified by natural language (i.e., ss). 2) The coding is evaluated separately by executing the generated solver-calling code block in an isolated subprocess, extracting the objective value, and comparing it to 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*}. Additional implementation details are provided in Appendix A.

Our goal is to find θ\theta that simultaneously maximize the quality of generated problems (e.g., validity and structural complexity, see Section 3.2) and the accuracy of solutions, by alternating RL updates to πθP\pi_{\theta}^{P} and πθS\pi_{\theta}^{S} over TT iterations. We describe the reward functions and training procedure in the following sections, while full prompts for both Proposer and the Solver are provided in Appendix B.

3.2  Proposer Reward Specification

At each iteration, the Proposer πθP\pi_{\theta}^{P} receives a prompt containing KK reference problems sampled from ℬ\mathcal{B} as in-context demonstrations, and is trained to generate 𝒫=(σ,f,𝒱,𝒞,s)\mathcal{P}=(\sigma,f,\mathcal{V},\mathcal{C},s) and the corresponding code implementation. The reference problems are used to enhance diversity: by varying the sampled references, we discourage the Proposer from collapsing to a small set of problem structures (e.g., a LP with 3 constraints) or limiting itself to specific application domains of ss (e.g., manufacturing).

The Proposer reward combines three factors via a gating formulation: RP=Rvalid×Rcorrect×RstructR^{P}=R_{\mathrm{valid}}\times R_{\mathrm{correct}}\times R_{\mathrm{struct}}. Here, Rvalid=𝕀⁡[𝒫​is parseable, feasible, bounded, and solved to optimality]R_{\mathrm{valid}}=\mathbb{I}[\mathcal{P}\ \text{is parseable, feasible, bounded, and solved to optimality}] is a hard validity gate. Given the objective value 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*} obtained from a canonical solver, Rcorrect∈{αc,1}R_{\mathrm{correct}}\in\{\alpha_{c},1\} checks whether the Proposer’s accompanying code correctly reproduces 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*}. Thus, invalid formulations receive zero reward, while valid formulations with incorrect code receive only a capped reward αc\alpha_{c}. For a valid and self-consistent problem, Rstruct∈[αs,1]R_{\mathrm{struct}}\in[\alpha_{s},1] measures whether the problem is structurally informative for Solver training. It is computed by the weighted combination of five scores, which capture active variable usage (svars_{\mathrm{var}}), non-trivial constraint count (scons_{\mathrm{con}}), coupling density (sdens_{\mathrm{den}}), variable coverage across constraints (scovs_{\mathrm{cov}}), and connectivity among constraints induced by shared variables (sgcs_{\mathrm{gc}}). These terms prioritize meaningful optimization structure over superficial size by penalizing duplicated components while rewarding coupled constraints that require relational reasoning among decision variables. The constant αs\alpha_{s} is a structural floor that prevents self-consistent problems from receiving a near-zero reward solely because they are simple early in training.

RstructR_{\mathrm{struct}} is not tied to a fixed notion of difficulty. After each iteration, newly generated problems are pre-scored by Solver rollouts, and medium-difficulty problems are used as an empirical estimate of the Solver’s current capability frontier (see Section 3.4). We update the structural target of RstructR_{\mathrm{struct}} from this frontier, so the Proposer is rewarded for generating problems that remain informative as the Solver improves, rather than merely increasing instance size or difficulty in an uncontrolled way. Full definitions of the Proposer reward and its update rule are deferred to Appendix C. We validate these design choices empirically. Section 4.2 shows that replacing the structured Proposer reward with a binary reward degrades performance, and Appendix F.7 shows that structural-reward GRPO outperforms a solve-rate-based baseline. These ablations suggest that optimization-specific, fine-grained structural feedback is more effective than coarse validity or solve-rate supervision alone.

3.3  Solver Reward Specification

The Solver πθS\pi_{\theta}^{S} receives only the natural-language description ss and must independently produce both a formal mathematical model and executable solver-calling code, without access to the Proposer’s formulation. The reward RSR^{S} is a weighted combination of two components, with wmw_{m} and wcw_{c} serving as weighting parameters, and is evaluated through independent verification pathways:

RS=wm​rmodel+wc​rcodeR^{S}=w_{m}r_{\mathrm{model}}+w_{c}r_{\mathrm{code}} (1)

Model score (rmodelr_{\mathrm{model}}). We compare the objective ff of Solver’s declared model (σ,f,𝒱,𝒞)(\sigma,f,\mathcal{V},\mathcal{C}) against 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*} obtained via our verification pipeline. To provide within-group variance for GRPO, we adopt a rule-based partial-credit scheme. Invalid or unparseable model outputs receive zero reward. Otherwise, the declared model is evaluated through a sequence of validation checks, including correctness of optimization sense, completeness of the objective and constraints, presence of explicit declared variables, dependence of the objective on decision variables, and successful canonical solving. Earlier failures receive smaller fixed rewards, with partial-credit values in {0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20}\{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20\} depending on the stage of failure. If the declared model passes all checks and is successfully solved, we further evaluate its objective correctness. The reward is defined below with an objective-match indicator ν\nu:

rmodel=wobj×ν+(1−wobj),ν(y,𝒫∗)=𝕀[|y−𝒫∗|≤max(ϵa,ϵr|𝒫∗|)],r_{\mathrm{model}}=w_{\text{obj}}\times\nu+(1-w_{\text{obj}}),\qquad\nu(y,\mathcal{P}^{*})=\mathbb{I}\!\left[|y-\mathcal{P}^{*}|\leq\max(\epsilon_{a},\epsilon_{r}|\mathcal{P}^{*}|)\right], (2)

where wobjw_{\text{obj}} controls the importance of objective matching, and ν=1\nu=1 when the declared model’s objective value yy matches 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*}. We use ϵr=10−2\epsilon_{r}=10^{-2} and ϵa=10−5\epsilon_{a}=10^{-5} during training-time verification.

Code score (rcoder_{\mathrm{code}}). The Solver’s generated code is executed in a sandboxed subprocess under a fixed time limit (i.e., 60ss). We assign a partial credit based on code execution outcome:

rcode={wobj×ν+(1−wobj)execution succeeds and an objective value is extracted,0.1code is present but fails to execute,0otherwise.r_{\mathrm{code}}=\begin{cases}w_{\text{obj}}\times\nu+(1-w_{\text{obj}})&\text{execution succeeds and an objective value is extracted,}\\ 0.1&\text{code is present but fails to execute,}\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (3)

A floor reward of 0.10.1 for failed execution ensures that the LLM is never discouraged from attempting code generation. Again, rmodelr_{\mathrm{model}} and rcoder_{\mathrm{code}} are evaluated through independent verification pathways (i.e., model formulation check and code execution check, respectively) so that the Solver must develop consistent reasoning for both model and code formulation rather than overfitting to either one alone.

3.4  Self-Play Training Loop

Both the Proposer and the Solver are optimized with the same GRPO objective (Guo et al., 2025), augmented with the clip-higher strategy, dynamic sampling, and token-level loss normalization from DAPO (Yu et al., 2025). The two roles differ only in prompt and reward definition: for the Proposer, a completion corresponds to a newly proposed optimization problem (with model formulation and code) and is scored by the proposer-specific reward RPR^{P}; for the Solver, a completion corresponds to candidate executable code to a given optimization problem and is scored by the solver-specific reward RSR^{S}. Concretely, given a prompt qq, we sample a group of GG completions {oi}i=1G\{o_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} from the current policy and update it with:

𝒥(θ)=𝔼q[1∑i=1G|oi|∑i=1G∑t=1|oi|min(ρi,tA^i,clip(ρi,t, 1−ϵ, 1+ϵ¯i)A^i)]−βDKL[πθ∥πref],\mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{q}\left[\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{G}|o_{i}|}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{t=1}^{|o_{i}|}\min\left(\rho_{i,t}\hat{A}_{i},\;\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\rho_{i,t},\,1-\epsilon,\,1+\bar{\epsilon}_{i}\right)\hat{A}_{i}\right)\right]-\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\right], (4)

where tt indexes tokens within oio_{i}; ρi,t=πθ​(oi,t∣q,oi,<t)πold​(oi,t∣q,oi,<t)\rho_{i,t}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(o_{i,t}\mid q,o_{i,<t})} is the token-level importance ratio between the current policy πθ\pi_{\theta} and the sampling policy πold\pi_{\mathrm{old}}, where πold\pi_{\mathrm{old}} denotes the policy checkpoint at the beginning of the current training iteration; RiR_{i} is the reward of oio_{i}, and A^i=(Ri−μr)/σr\hat{A}_{i}=(R_{i}-\mu_{r})/\sigma_{r} is the group-normalized advantage computed from rewards of the GG completions. μr\mu_{r} and σr\sigma_{r} denote the within-group mean and standard deviation, respectively; ϵ\epsilon is the base clipping coefficient; and ϵ¯i=ϵh𝟏[A^i>0]+ϵ𝟏[A^i≤0]\bar{\epsilon}_{i}=\epsilon_{h}\mathbf{1}[\hat{A}_{i}>0]+\epsilon\mathbf{1}[\hat{A}_{i}\leq 0] is the asymmetric upper clipping bound with ϵh>ϵ\epsilon_{h}>\epsilon. Moreover, the KL (Kullback-Leibler) penalty with coefficient β\beta constrains updates relative to policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}.

Since both problem proposal and problem solving exhibit sparse and highly prompt-dependent rewards, using group-relative advantages removes prompt-level reward scale variation and makes training depend on the relative quality of completions within the same context. Normalizing by the total number of generated tokens stabilizes the overall update scale across groups with different completion lengths, which is important because both Proposer and Solver generations vary substantially in length. The clip-higher modification allows larger policy improvements on high-reward completions while keeping conservative updates on weaker ones, which is especially helpful during early training when successful trajectories are rare. As in DAPO, we discard groups whose GG completions receive identical rewards, since such groups yield zero relative advantage and provide no learning signal. At each iteration tt, training proceeds in four stages, as presented by Algorithm 1 in Appendix D.

Stage 1: Proposer Training. We construct a proposer training set 𝒟tP\mathcal{D}_{t}^{P} of NPN_{P} examples, each consisting of a prompt that includes KK reference problems sampled from the current buffer ℬt−1\mathcal{B}_{t-1} to encourage diversity (K=0K=0 in the first iteration). The Proposer (πθt−1P\pi^{P}_{\theta_{t-1}}) is then updated with GRPO on 𝒟tP\mathcal{D}_{t}^{P} using reward RPR^{P}, producing intermediate parameters θ~t\tilde{\theta}_{t}, where RPR^{P} is defined in Section 3.2.

Stage 2: Proposer Generation and Pre-scoring. The updated Proposer πθ~tP\pi^{P}_{\tilde{\theta}_{t}} generates N^\hat{N} candidate problems with objective values obtained through the solver-grounded verification process described in Section 3.1. Each valid candidate pp is pre-scored using HH independent rollouts from the Solver. Reusing the objective-matching indicator ν\nu defined in Eq. 2, we define:

ρ^​(p)=1H​∑h=1Hν⁡(yh,𝒫∗),\hat{\rho}(p)=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\nu(y_{h},\mathcal{P}^{*}), (5)

where yhy_{h} is the objective value returned by the hh-th Solver rollout; failed executions are assigned ν⁡(yh,𝒫∗)=0\nu(y_{h},\mathcal{P}^{*})=0. Problems are then classified into difficulty categories based on solve rate ρ^\hat{\rho}:

d⁡(p)={hard,0<ρ^​(p)≤0.25medium,0.25<ρ^​(p)≤0.75easy,0.75<ρ^​(p)<1d(p)=\begin{cases}\text{hard},&0<\hat{\rho}(p)\leq 0.25\\ \text{medium},&0.25<\hat{\rho}(p)\leq 0.75\\ \text{easy},&0.75<\hat{\rho}(p)<1\end{cases} (6)

Stage 3: Buffer Update. After pre-scoring, we retain only problems that are valid and informative for subsequent learning. In particular, we discard problems with ρ^​(p)=0\hat{\rho}(p)=0, which provides no reliable training signal, as well as trivial problems with ρ^​(p)=1\hat{\rho}(p)=1, which are already fully mastered by the current Solver. The remaining problems are admitted into the reference buffer ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t}, a capped repository of previously generated instances used for both Proposer prompting and Solver training. To prevent learning collapse toward a narrow set of templates, we impose a structural deduplication that limits the number of problems sharing the same signature, including the problem family, number of variables, number of constraints, and optimization sense. When the buffer exceeds its maximum capacity |ℬ|max|\mathcal{B}|_{\max}, entries are evicted based on their estimated training value, with easier instances removed before medium ones and medium instances removed before harder ones, ensuring that ℬ\mathcal{B} remains concentrated on diverse and sufficiently challenging problems.

Stage 4: Solver Training and Difficulty Refresh. We construct the Solver training set 𝒟tS\mathcal{D}_{t}^{S} from two complementary sources: newly generated problems retained after pre-scoring and problems sampled from the reference buffer ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t}. The new problems make Solver updates responsive to the evolving Proposer, while buffer replay helps mitigate short-term distribution drift and maintain coverage of previously discovered problem families. Specifically, 80% of the samples in 𝒟tS\mathcal{D}_{t}^{S} are drawn from the current iteration’s retained problems, while the remaining 20% are sampled from ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t}. Both sources are sampled according to the fixed difficulty-aware distribution (weasy,wmed,whard)=(0.2,0.3,0.5)(w_{\text{easy}},w_{\text{med}},w_{\text{hard}})=(0.2,0.3,0.5), which prioritizes harder instances. Starting from the intermediate parameters θ~t\tilde{\theta}_{t}, the Solver is updated with GRPO on 𝒟tS\mathcal{D}_{t}^{S} using reward RSR^{S}, producing the end-of-iteration parameters θt\theta_{t}. After Solver training, we refresh the empirical solve-rate estimates and difficulty labels of replayed buffer problems using the rollouts collected during this training stage. These rollout-based estimates provide an online approximation of problem difficulty relative to the evolving Solver.

4  Experiments

We instantiate OPT-Zero from Qwen3-8B-Base and optimize it with GRPO using the ms-swift. We run 15 self-play iterations, using 64 Proposer prompts and 64 Solver training samples per iteration. We evaluate on 6 datasets: NL4Opt (Ramamonjison et al., 2023), MAMO-EasyLP (Huang et al., 2024), MAMO-ComplexLP (Huang et al., 2024), NLP4LP (AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024), IndustryOR (IndOR) (Huang et al., 2025), and ReSocratic (Yang et al., 2025b), which are widely used benchmarks, with details provided in prior literature (Xiao et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026). We report Pass@1 accuracy, defined as the proportion of test instances for which a single generated program returns the correct objective value. We report per-dataset results and the macro- and micro-average metrics across all benchmarks. More details of experiment settings are provided in Appendix E.

We consider three types of baselines, including zero-shot LLMs, inference-time methods, and fine-tuned LLMs. Zero-shot LLMs include OpenAI o4-mini (OpenAI, 2025), DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025), GLM-5 (Zeng et al., 2026), Google Gemma4-31B, Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025a). Inference-time methods (all based on GPT-4o) include OptiMUS (AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024), Chain-of-Thought (CoT) strategy (Wei et al., 2022), Chain-of-Experts (CoE) (Xiao et al., 2024), and CAFA (Deng et al., 2024). For fine-tuned LLMs, we compare against ORLM (Huang et al., 2025), LLMOPT (Jiang et al., 2025a), OR-PRM (Wang et al., 2026), EVOM (Guan et al., 2026), SIRL (Chen et al., 2025a), and StepORLM (Zhou et al., 2026). Since OPT-Zero can be extended by introducing existing dataset during Solver training, we also report results of this enhanced version (OPT-Zero-D), which samples 30% problems per iteration from training set of Chen et al. (2025a).

4.1  Main Results

Table 2 compares OPT-Zero with all baselines on six benchmarks. Remarkably, although OPT-Zero is only an 8B model, it outperforms substantially larger general-purpose LLMs such as GLM-5 (744B), as well as prompt-based inference methods built on GPT-4o. Example Proposer generations and Solver solutions of OPT-Zero are provided in Appendix F.1 and Appendix F.2, respectively.

Even without using any expert-annotated data for fine-tuning, OPT-Zero surpasses most data-dependent approaches and reaches performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods such as StepORLM. In particular, among fine-tuned LLMs, OPT-Zero achieves new state-of-the-art results on IndustryOR (54.8) and ReSocratic (89.8). Further finetuned by a small amount of data (only problem description and optimal objectives), the micro-average performance of OPT-Zero-D surpasses all previous methods. Importantly, unlike prior SFT-based methods, these gains do not come at the cost of general-purpose reasoning capabilities (see Appendix F.3). In addition, we also evaluate the generalizability of the trained model to other optimization solvers in Appendix F.4, where we find OPT-Zero exhibits strong zero-shot transferability, which existing state-of-the-art methods fail to demonstrate. These results highlight the potential of OPT-Zero in overcoming the issue of generalization ceiling. Finally, Appendix F.5 shows that OPT-Zero can further benefit from inference-time scaling, leading to additional performance gains beyond the single-sample setting.

4.2  Ablation Studies

To assess the contribution of each component, we evaluate five variants of OPT-Zero: 1) w/o Solver training; 2) w/o Proposer training; 3) w/o Reference buffer, where no buffer is used in either the Proposer prompts or the Solver training; 4) w. Binary Solver reward, where the structured Solver reward is replaced by a binary signal, assigning 1 for correct generations and 0 for all other outputs; and 5) w. Binary Proposer reward, which applies the same binary scheme to the Proposer.

As shown in Table 3, removing any major component or simplifying the reward consistently hurts performance, confirming the effectiveness of our methodological design. The largest accuracy drops come from removing Solver training or replacing its structured reward with a binary signal, indicating that Solver training is central to solving optimization problems. Proposer training and its structured reward also improve Solver performance, clearly suggesting beneficial mutual interaction between the two roles. The reference buffer is likewise important, as it helps the Proposer generate harder problems while providing useful problem-distribution memory for Solver learning.

In addition, we further investigate the choice of sampling weights in the difficulty-aware Solver training process in Appendix F.6, as well as the use of structural reward in Proposer RL in Appendix F.7.

4.3  Discussion

Learning to Use Different Solvers. As a generalizable framework, OPT-Zero can be applied to train LLMs to use a variety of solvers and optimization languages. Beyond Gurobi, we train Qwen3-8B-Base to interact with CPLEX via DOcplex, SCIP via PySCIPOpt, and Pyomo. Figure 3 compares the performance of Qwen3-8B-Base and our trained models. According to the figure, while the degree of improvement differs, OPT-Zero consistently enhances model performance across different solvers. More importantly, since these improvements are obtained by training with the target solver, we further verify zero-shot transferability of OPT-Zero across solvers in Appendix F.4.

Synergy between Proposer and Solver. The Proposer and Solver are designed to learn cooperatively through shared parameters. To examine how the Solver benefits the Proposer, we track the correctness rate (i.e., Rcorrect=1R_{\mathrm{correct}}=1) of the N^\hat{N} problems generated by the Proposer at each iteration in Figure 4. Training the Solver alone already improves Proposer correctness, while jointly training both roles achieves the best performance, indicating effective knowledge transfer through shared parameters. Conversely, to examine how the Proposer benefits the Solver, Table 3 shows that Solver-only training underperforms joint training by a clear margin (75.1 vs. 81.6 Macro Avg.), suggesting that Proposer training supplies more informative problem instances for Solver improvement.

Generalizability to Different LLMs. In Appendix F.8, we demonstrate that the gains of our method persist across LLMs with different architectures and sizes, suggesting that the improvement is not tied to a particular base model. Instead, it provides adaptive supervision that scales with the LLM’s current modeling frontier, mitigating capability anchoring to a static training dataset.

5  Conclusion

We present OPT-Zero, a framework that enables LLMs to master optimization tasks without relying on human-annotated data. By iteratively training dual roles (i.e., a Proposer and a Solver) through RL, OPT-Zero establishes a self-play loop that progressively enhances LLMs in optimization reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OPT-Zero achieves competitive performance among LLM-based frameworks, significantly outperforming the backbone model on diverse benchmark tasks.

Future directions include: 1) extending the framework to broader problem classes, such as nonlinear programming and stochastic programming; 2) developing more refined reward mechanisms (e.g., training a reward model) to better assess Proposer and Solver outputs; 3) integrating solver-calling code generation with automated heuristic discovery to further amplify optimization performance.
